item.title: Where are the adults in AI safety?
item.description:
The following is based on a true story (not mine).

Let’s say you’ve been bombarded with enough AI doom that you decide to do something about it! You watched Artificial and don’t trust the frontier labs to steer us somewhere safe on their own, so you want to work on the problem from the outside. You’re a little fuzzy on the acronyms - AGI, RSI, TAI, SVU - but by God you’re going to figure it out.

So, you Google “How to get into AI safety.” And it’s encouraging! There are articles about how AI safety needs founders. There are calls for technical people to switch careers. There are career transition grants, which sound like money to stop doing your meaningless and/or actively destructive job and start saving the world. “Great, that’s me!” you think, and so you apply.

Within 24 hours you get a rejection email in your inbox: “Hey, we’re so happy you want to save the world. It’s the most important issue of our generation! But we don’t think you can help. Why don’t you try taking my course or reading my LessWrong articles or listen to my podcast or follow me on twitter first? Thanks!”

Huh. Maybe it’s because you used an AI to edit your answers. You’d think this field, of all fields, would have made its peace with that. Maybe you’re just not that good. Fine. So, you take the seemingly automated email’s advice and sign up for a course from the color-shape company, to learn and meet like-minded people.

A few hours after signing up - err, applying? they don’t just let you sign up - another email lands. Someone from that organization thinks you’re super talented and they’d love to get you involved in AI safety. Can you hop on a call?

A little confused, you hop on a call. It goes like this:

Them: We’d love to get you involved.

You: Great. How can I get involved?

Them: I don’t know. We’ll think about that. Have you thought about applying for a career transition grant?

You: I did. I got rejected.

Them: Oh, that’s so funny. You’re the perfect person for it.

You: It was a very fast rejection.

Them: Hmm. Let me look into that.

You: Great. I’m going to take a course and keep learning more - could we touch base in a couple of weeks?

Them: Maybe, but I’d really need you to justify why that would be a good use of my time. How it would maximize my impact.

You: Oh, ok...

You get off the call, bewildered. You’ve been in corporate environments before, had passive aggressive co-workers and been ghosted by people far more senior than you, but this is a first. Nobody has ever asked you to make the business case for a 15-minute chat that they started.

It doesn’t help to know who is on the other end of this call. It’s not a chief executive squeezing you in between board meetings or an expert running to testify for Congress. It’s a 24-year-old who graduated college two years ago, has never managed anyone, has never worked a regular job, and has somehow ended up gatekeeping the field recruiting people to save the world. This person is so focused on maximizing their impact that they’re willing to minimize it by being a huge dick to someone THEY emailed.

And it keeps happening. You apply to do technical research and hear back that you aren’t technical enough. You apply to incubators, which ask you to prove how much you care before they ask what you can do. Meanwhile the people running these programs continue to go on podcasts and write posts about how AI safety needs more founders.

I mean. It does! That’s the frustrating part. And you want to be one of them! Ahhhhhhhh!

…

Here is my current demography of AI safety. There are three generations:

  1. The grandparents. They’ve been worried about AI for 15-20 years, since AI was but a twinkle in Sam Altman’s eye. They were right about AI being within reach in our lifetimes - a far from consensus opinion - which is a real achievement, and now they’re too important for day-to-day work. They’re also kind of grouchy. In fact, quite grouchy. In fact, being curmudgeons is what pre-disposed them to be worriers, and it makes them not very charismatic.
  2. The adults. These are the people who were working professionals eight or ten years ago, often already in tech, and who cared about this stuff or lied well enough to convince a “mission driven non-profit” that they did. They went to the labs. They’re at Anthropic and OpenAI - or have left to build a harness or sandbox of some kind - and they’re pretty busy and doing quite well financially.
  3. The kids. They’re 24, and they run a lot of the courses, grants and incubators that decide who gets to help save the world. They’ve been gloomy and anxious about existential risk since they were 16, with an enormous sense of urgency and a view that managing other people’s feelings is a distraction from the mission.

All of these archetypes feed into the communication problem in AI at large and AI safety specifically by constantly contradicting themselves. The grandparents say “everyone should be working on this, or we'll die” and then tell Nick Cammarata his research is a dead end and will never solve alignment. The adults say “this technology might kill everyone, please regulate us” while IPOing at $2T and launching an AI-native Microsoft Office. The kids say, “AI safety needs startups!" but then screen outsiders and who could get up to speed and go found impactful companies.

For example, here’s a question from the application for an introductory AI safety course:

Oh, you haven’t done 18 fellowships? I guess you can’t join! I get that they have to screen some people out, but the system is essentially built to make outsiders prove they’re already insiders.

I have a theory for why this might be. The kids made this form, and it’s a reflection of the scholastic environment they grew up in.

In middle school they did the activity that got them into the right high school club. The club got them into the right college, where there was another club, with its own application, that got them an internship. Rung after rung existed to get you to the next rung. Peter Thiel has been complaining about this for years: the smartest kids spend their twenties competing ferociously for conventional prizes, and what they learn is mostly how to compete.

So, when the kids were handed a field to run, they built a ladder. There’s an intro course, with an application. The course gets you ready for the fellowship, which gets you a grant so you can do research for the next fellowship, so on and so forth.

It’s sad. They had to go through all that and nobody ever told them it was bullshit. And as a result, they’ve built AI safety as a ladder to nowhere.

…

So, who is AI safety screening for, really?

One of my favorite ideas from when I worked in the criminal legal system is that there’s no such thing as a broken system, and really, you should think of every system as perfectly designed to get the results it produces. Our legal system, for example, is well designed to create mass incarceration if that’s what you want.

The best contrast for AI safety is the legendary adolescent daycare, Y Combinator. YC gets ~80,000 applications a year for ~800 spots, and their final interview is only 10 minutes. They believe that 10 minutes is enough to capture the nascent Steve Jobs and Elon Musks of the world. If that doesn’t feel true, they re-design the process.

I have mixed feelings about Y Combinator and I’m sure it misses plenty of people. But at the very least, they’re intentional about what they’re screening for and try not to make it unduly burdensome on themselves or their applicants.

But AI safety. Steve Jobs at 21 is a Reed College dropout whose main credential is a calligraphy class. He has no PhD in alignment research. He has never worked at a lab. He has spent zero hours on AI safety and knows nobody he could ask for a referral. What he has is breadth, and recombinant innovation - a knack for pulling from different fields and combining them into something new.

He’d fit in today’s AI safety ecosystem like a failed organ transplant - quickly and decisively rejected (then asked to justify any further 15-minute calls based on his potential impact).

AI safety is designed to produce people who are good at getting into AI safety programs, fellowship hopping, learning the lexicon. It’s not designed, however, to recruit it’s stated preference for a founder archetype.

What makes a founder useful is mostly temperament and a willingness to learn. A lot of the time those people aren’t PhD researchers. They come from other fields and they’ve built things on their own, with mixed results. AI safety screens for technical depth and philosophical fluency, which is right if you’re hiring for the bottom right corner of the chart below.


Here’s the thing about the people who get screened out: they don’t go home. Someone willing to quit their job to work on AI is going to work on AI. The only question is which door is open.

So, there you are, rejected, purity tested and asked to justify 15 minutes of someone else’s time. You still care, and you still want real experience with this technology. And there is one place that will take a competent adult without asking how many fellowships they’ve done: a frontier lab’s deployment company, which embeds engineers inside big companies to get the models into production faster. They interview you like a normal company. They call you back. Nobody asks you to justify the call.

You take the job. You’ll do safety from the inside! And maybe launch the startup you dreamt up in a year or two, when you have a better network and more experience.

In the meantime, you’re pretty busy and handsomely compensated. But you're still scared, somewhere deep inside, so you go on X and call for pacing the frontier. You go to bed feeling like a responsible adult.

item.title: Giving Up on Saving the World
item.description:
When I was 19, I decided I was going to save the world.

Now, 25 years later, I’ve decided to give up.

To explain why and what giving up means, we first need to go back to how I ever got into the world-saving business. As a kid, I loved computers, and I started teaching myself to program them when I was 8. By 16 I could write real programs that did interesting things, and it was also around this time I got into Linux. And since I was into Linux, that meant I read Slashdot.

If you weren’t into Linux in the late 90s, you might not even know what Slashdot was. It still exists, but it’s a shell of its former self. Back then it was a vibrant, community-driven news site that in many important ways felt to me like LessWrong feels now. And it was from Slashdot that I learned about nanotech and grey goo, which led me to the Foresight Institute, which led me to the Extropians, which ultimately led to me being a very early member of the SL4 mailing list.

And, again, if you’re not familiar with SL4, it’s approximately how all this AI safety and rationalist stuff got started. And so it was sometime over the summer of 2001, discussing Friendly AI with Eliezer Yudkowsky on IRC, that I decided to orient my life around saving the world from the risks of superintelligent AI.

The only problem was, I wasn’t up to the task yet. In fact, nobody was. In that first decade I, along with everyone else, was just trying to figure out how to think well enough to be able to think usefully about AI at all. It proved a surprisingly hard task, and one that required the founding of the rationalist community.

While all this was happening, I was also living my life. I stayed in school for a while trying for a math PhD, then dropped out, joined a startup, and got married. When the startup and the marriage failed, I took the chance to move to the Bay Area. This was in 2013, and the rationalist community was starting to come together in person. I moved into a rationalist group house in Berkeley, took a job with another startup, and on nights and weekends worked on my “hobby” of figuring out how to save the world.

Over time, I came up with some ideas. I wrote a lot about them. I still think some of them are pretty good ideas that are worth exploring more. They might even contribute to world saving. But by 2020 it was clear to me I was less interested in AI safety engineering (at least as it existed at that time) and more interested in philosophy, so I pivoted to writing Fundamental Uncertainty, a book about all the philosophy I’d had to work out to think clearly about AI. My hope was still that I’d save the world, but I’d do it by enabling other people to work effectively in AI safety. I finished that book earlier this year, and then the question became, what should I do next?

Life conspired for a while to keep me from answering that question. I suffered my fourth concussion in July and have had post-concussion syndrome since then. I’m close to being back to normal, but still not completely there. I also took on a larger role at work, and while I think what we’re doing is important, it’s obviously not saving the world from AI-induced catastrophe. So between concussion recovery and work, I’ve not had a lot of time to do anything extra, and in that time the world has also changed.

The timeline to superintelligence is looking short. At the moment, the most likely world-saving activities are in policy and politics, two areas I’ve long shied away from. I do what I can. I write and call my representatives. I engage on Twitter. I do my best to be a link in preference cascade chains that may lead to effective policy outcomes.

But between the changes in my life and changes in the world, I’ve had to accept that I’m not going to be the one to save the world, and it’s time I stopped trying. And that’s okay, because it’s not up to one person to save it. Reality isn’t like a Marvel movie or a fairytale. The future of the world doesn’t hang—or only does very rarely—on the actions of a single person. Instead, it’s the actions of many people working together that have saved the world. That’s how we managed to keep the ozone layer, stop acid rain, prevent nuclear war, engineer our way out of Y2K, and much else.

And so I think I can finally say, after spending more than half my life trying to save the world, that I’ve given up. Not on the world being saved, but on saving the world on my own.

I want to be clear that I do still think we can save the world, and that the world needs saving, specifically from the threat posed by superintelligent AI. It’s just that such saving is unlikely to happen because one person did one thing, but instead because many people did many things to avert myriad potential catastrophes. So although I’m giving up on saving the world, I’m not giving up on the world being saved, and I’ll do what I can to contribute to that effort.

item.title: Easier To Be Good
item.description:
I do not consider myself a good person. I am lazy and frivolous and inconsiderate, I care too much about intelligence and status, I am a snob and a hypocrite, and I do not call my mother enough.

I don't mean this to read as self-hatred, nor a show of false modesty. Among all the people I know there is only a scant handful of people I would consider genuinely good, and so it is unremarkable to me that I wouldn't find myself amongst their number.

You do not need to be good to desire more goodness in the world. It is good for everyone when things are good, and when there is more of it — more thoughtfulness, more generosity, more coordination, more care, more beauty, more clarity, more positive sum trades, more sophistication and elegance in our solutions and resolutions.

Increasing the amount of goodness in the world is an urgent project. The world really sucks right now, and even in the wealthiest enclaves of the imperial core there is an immense amount of suffering.

To reach the healed world would be a massive complicated undertaking. It is such a massive complicated undertaking that it is not enough for only those who are intrinsically good to work on it. There simply aren’t enough of them.

If it is desirable (as I contend) for morally mediocre people like me to work on the project, it would not be enough to appeal to their innate goodness, for they have not that much of it to be appealed to. You will need to offer me things that are more base, like status and money and the affirmation that I am a good person (for everyone wants to be a virtuous person and to be recognized as such, whether or not they are).

Fortuitously, there was an instructive breakthrough around a decade ago: effective altruism. Here's approximately what that is: you take people who come from the morally bankrupt culture that is the western professional managerial class, and you give us the prestige and status and affirmation of virtue we neurotically crave for the trivial cost of ten percent of our income and a few weekends a year where we are subject to vegan food and like sixteen hours of one-on-one discussions with a bunch of earnest dorks. As a result, suddenly a contingent of this culture begins to compete in a new arena of QALYs and utilons and eyestalk ablation literature reviews rather than the traditional arena of summer home square footage and the number of Michelin star restaurants one has set foot in.

Put it that way, and it doesn't sound so different from the beautiful promise of capitalism: that if we can successfully align the system with human values, it will result in some sort of elegant virtuous cycle such that people can go about selfishly pursuing their self-interested goals, and end up pouring immense amounts of goodness into the world as a side product.

As a mediocre person, it does sure seem self-evident to me that the only way to get mediocre people to do good, en masse, is to generate more selfish incentives for doing so. Whether capitalism has successfully done that is discoursebait I will leave to more foolhardy poasters.[1] What I know for sure is that effective altruism did this for me. I dedicate much more of my energy and my money towards the reduction of suffering of sentient beings than I otherwise would, by a really really really wide margin.

It did this by not only appealing to some of my best instincts, but also some of my ugly ones, and ones that are simply mammalian. The community gave me peers that respected me and pushed me towards more virtuousness. I have recognition for my talents, and social status, and the occasional extra bag of money bit of funding when I do things that are unusually aligned with their goals. Insofar as engaging in effective altruism makes me do more improving things for the world than I would otherwise, it seems wise to continue to engage with it: to reap all of the rewards and allow myself to enjoy them to the fullest without guilt, such that I have as much motivation as I can get to continue to do good things for the world.

I am impure, so perhaps it is unsurprising that I've always disliked purity in my politics. Stringent, inhuman standards do not seem to me like the most effective way to increase the amount of goodness in the world. More specifically, stringent, inhuman standards will get you the small minority of humans who are inhumanly virtuous, and leave the rest of us out. To me that feels like leaving resources on the table.

I am not a good person, but I am a better one than I was before people started paying me in tangibles and intangibles to act like one. I would like as many people as possible to experience this privilege. For that to be the case, we will need to be thoughtful about how to bring more people into the fold — how to create a culture in which it is easier for people to be good.

  1. ^

    ...And my footnotes. I recognize that neither capitalism or the effective altruist ecosystem is as well aligned as its ideal versions would be, but this does not overly trouble me. Alignment problems of all kinds are wicked and difficult, and it makes sense to me that the very complicated ones (that won’t kill us imminently) might take up to centuries to straighten out. As long as there is continual improvement, I feel okay with the slowness of the bend towards justice.

item.title: Bayesian Games with Nukes
item.description:
How we all learned to stop worrying and love the bomb... for a while

Listen to this post on the Non-Zero-Sum James podcast

Nearing the end of 1961 the Soviet Union tested a 50-megaton hydrogen bomb equivalent to 3800 Hiroshima bombs. At the same time an intelligence officer by the name of Juanita Moody and her team became aware of Soviet ships delivering large cargo, under cover of darkness in Cuba—what if such a bomb was being delivered to the doorstep of the US?

A surprise attack of that magnitude, would devastate the US, and potentially destroy its ability to retaliate, jeopardising the offensive standoff between the Soviets and the US that would come to be known as...

M.A.D: An Easy (Albeit High-Stakes) Problem

One of the strangest dynamics in geopolitical history has to be that of Mutually Assured Destruction (M.A.D.), it is almost as crazy as its name suggests.

"Two superpowers, the U.S. and U.S.S.R., represent such enormous destructive potentials as to afford little chance of a purely passive equilibrium"

—John Von Neumann

The father of game theory, John Von Neumann correctly identified that a passive approach to nuclear war would not result in a peaceful equilibrium, instead a mutually aggressive stance counter-intuitively lead to the long-running stand off that was the Cold War, and except for a few close calls, humanity found an unlikely saviour. Miraculously, mutual aggression with apocalyptic weaponry has shepherded the world through the most peaceful period in recorded history.

Deterrence is the art of producing in the mind of the enemy... the fear to attack.

—Dr Strangelove

The US and the Soviet Union's automatic defense systems acted as a literal doomsday device* meaning that a launch by an aggressor would lead to both countries being destroyed and a nuclear winter that might kill all life on earth. The perfect apocalyptic deterrent was lampooned in Stanley Kubrick's "Dr Strangelove" when the Soviet Ambassador reveals that they have created one, but haven't announced it to the public yet.

"The... whole point of the doomsday machine... is lost... if you keep it a secret!"

—Dr Strangelove

A doomsday device makes any offensive action (defection) on either side lead to the end of the world, making cooperation the dominant strategy. The conclusion, put in pithy terms in the 80s movie "War Games" by Joshua (the artificially intelligent computer) was:

The only way to win is not to play.

In game theoretical terms, MAD is a simple complete information game. I think of it as a comfortable local minimum, at the top of a precipitous drop.

But when Moody discovered the subs delivering unknown cargo in Cuba, stepping outside of her NSA remit to implore military officials to act (stepping on the toes of the CIA, whose job it is to determine military advice), that all changed. Moody's discovery made a stable equilibrium, into a Bayesian Game: A game with imperfect information—players don't know enough to make a definitive deduction, they are required make judgments based on probability, and then to update their positions based on real time information. A much less stable situation.

What Are Bayesian Games?

Thomas Bayes was an 18th century mathematician who devised a theorem to update probabilities based on new information. Bayesian games were developed in the 1960s by economist John Harsanyi using Bayesian probability to solve games with incomplete information.

Bayesian Reasoning

A simple contemporary example of Bayesian reasoning is vaccination efficacy during the Covid Pandemic.

I remember at one point, vaccine hesitant critics were pointing to the fact that we were seeing the same amount of vaccinated people being hospitalised with Covid as unvaccinated, seeming to suggest that the vaccine was ineffective. But take a moment to apply some Bayesian reasoning and you find that, given additional information this is off by a long shot.

The important piece of information to add is that, at the time, we had a 90% vaccination rate. So, for every 10 people, 9 were vaccinated and 1 was not and yet these groups were generating the same amount of hospitalisations. So, an unvaccinated person was 9 x more likely to end up hospitalised than a vaccinated person. Meaning the effectiveness of the vaccine was ~89%

This example gives a sense of the dramatic difference updating probabilities can make. Introducing a new factor can completely upend the calculus.

Hawks & Doves... & Chickens

As Dr Strangelove correctly identified, it is the knowledge of the Doomsday Device that makes it an effective deterrent. All you need to assume of your opponent is that they're not suicidal. While there are two Nash equilibria for Mutually Assured Destruction, there is only one strategy that is not suicidal; cooperate†.

But when you don't know if one side has first strike capacity then the mutual destruction is no longer assured—introducing a host of unknowns. Can they wipe out our capacity to retaliate? If they can will they? Do they love their children too? (much of my knowledge on the Cuban Missile crisis originates from the song "Russians" by Sting). In short: are they hawks or doves?

And this was no empty concern. The US knew the Soviets would consider a first strike because the US had done so themselves. In the 5 years before the USSR reached parity with the US (while the US had the atomic bomb and the Soviets did not) the hawkish John Von Neumann along with serious contemporary thinkers like Bertrand Russel advocated for the game-theory-optimal move—a strong legitimate threat of nuclear strike on Russia unless they ceased their own development of nuclear weapons.

Ironically this game-theory optimal move may have put the world in a much more precarious position than the counterintuitive standoff achieved by M.A.D. These Bayesian considerations are what comprised...

The Cuban Missile Crisis

"Mr Khrushchev says he will bury you, I don't subscribe to this point of view"

—Sting

What drove the world into crisis were the new unknowns involved, the Bayesian factors. And in the end, the result of this global game of chicken, and the world's survival depended, not on the systemic pressures at play, but instead on the actions of a handful of people: Juanita Moody, without whom the threat might have gone unnoticed until it was too late, Kennedy and Khrushchev whose contrasting public rhetoric and private correspondence balanced appearances and reality, and one senior Russian submarine officer Vasili Arkipov.

When the Soviets shot down a U-2 plane over Cuba, killing the US pilot, Kennedy, advised by his military staff, made plans to strike back but refrained—hostilities were on a knife's edge. At one stage a US aircraft carrier the USS Randolph attempted to force a nuclear-armed Soviet submarine to surface using depth charges. The submarine's Captain Valentin Savitsky having no idea whether the charges were meant as a warning or as an attack, and his radar showing more US ships closing in, ordered the submarine's ten kiloton nuclear torpedo to be prepared for launch. The torpedo, if fired would completely vaporise the USS Randolph, and quickly trigger attacks on Russia's targets in Europe.

With their nuclear payload armed and ready—permission to fire required the consent of all three senior officers on board. Facing the threat of a war they believed had already begun, two of the three officers gave their permission to fire, Arkhipov alone refused, insisting they wait for further information.

When they surfaced the submarine, they found all was quiet, it was not the end of the world.

Finally, on the morning of October 28, after a pleading letter was received from Khrushchev, the United States secretly offered to remove its nuclear missile bases in Turkey and Italy, Khrushchev agreed to dismantle the missile sites in Cuba. The worst of the crisis was over, the world had escaped armageddon, MAD-ness was restored.

While the Cold War involved many proxy conflicts with the Soviets and US vying for "Containment", there has not been direct conflict between nuclear powers since 1945.

But those were simpler times.

A New Nuclear Crisis?

The delicate balance was held because we had two players with identical responses, and identical access to each other. But like during the Cuban Missile Crisis, the landscape has changed, there are many nuclear powers now and shifting possibilities with AI and cyber warfare, as well as potentially apocalyptic bio-weapons, have unsettled this balance, for the last few years many prominent geopolitical commentators have been worrying out loud about the re-emergence of the nuclear threat.

Much like the 'three body problem', we've gone from a regular, predictable pattern between two major players, to multiple "bodies" creating the conditions for chaos.

We're seeing it in film and TV too, with stories like "A House Built on Dynamite" and "Paradise". These sorts of problems are what are called...

Multipolar Traps: Hard Problems

People have begun to frame AI in the same terms as the nuclear threat, most pointedly in the title of Nate Soares and Eliezer Yudkowsky's book.

If anyone builds it, everyone dies.

This might suggest a sense of a new M.A.D. for AI, but there are so many "bodies" involved in the AI race that if we can't rely on this strong polarised balance to safeguard against this threat of AI. We don't stand a snowflakes chance in hell of keeping AI balanced in this way.

We are already seeing AI agents "killing" each other (halting their processes, denying access) when given prompts to seek out the most trivial limited resources like concert tickets. In this Wes Roth video he explains that more powerful models like Mythos take a "first strike" approach in these conflicts, gaining dominance before cooperating (forced compliance). So, we are seeing, in current LLM models, the emergence of hawkish game-theoretical strategies that might be disastrous.

So...

M.A.D. demonstrates how counter-intuitively mutual aggression can lead to a peaceful conflict, and how introducing unknowns can upset that balance making conflict more likely. In the case of the Cuban Missile Crisis, this imbalance meant that the fate of the world fell to just a few human beings, with all their flaws, rule breaking, emotions, irrational motivations, in short, with their humanity. Who knows if one of those humans had been swapped-out for a perfectly rational robot following rules and making game-theory optimal decisions, whether the result would have been different.

When we weigh artificial super-intelligence's own risks with the re-emergence of the nuclear threat, what was for a while an easy problem now becomes a multi-polar trap. Combine this with all the other interdependent crises from climate to inequality and you have a massive coordination problem that Daniel Schmactenberger calls the Meta-Crisis—which is where we're going next.

Continue the Series

  • The Dividual Strikes Back—why nothing and everything is your fault
  • What Is the Meta-Crisis?—the mother of all coordination problems

Notes

  • * A doomsday device was first imagined by physicist Leo Szilard (famous for postulating nuclear chain-reactions) in 1950—his hypothetical "Cobalt Bomb"—a hydrogen bomb wrapped in cobalt, would, on detonation, generate enough enduring nuclear fallout to kill all life on earth. It was later formalised by Herman Khan at RAND as a doomsday machine.
  • † This is a bit of a technical point, I actually think this might be an oversight by Nash, in that there is an asymmetry in gauging the equilibria. The only stipulation is that there be no benefit to deviating from your strategy, but it doesn't account for the corollary that there might be no cost to deviating. At which point it makes the choice moot. So, in the case of MAD, there's never a motivation to defect, because there's no benefit to defecting even if the other defects.

Originally published at nonzerosum.games, illustrated with hand-drawn cartoons and interactive elements.

item.title: Alignment 'train/test splits' should be sacred
item.description:
Tl;dr: Alignment techniques can be used for training alignment or for testing it, but they cannot be used for both! As we build out the set of alignment techniques available to us, we should enforce that some are judiciously reserved only for evaluating alignment.

See also: Validating against a misalignment detector is very different to training against one.

Here is a guiding principle regarding alignment-minded AI training: whatever you do, you must maximally avoid teaching the model to take misaligned actions which are invisible to the user. In fact, you should be shamed if you use training techniques which encourage covert misalignment.

Here is a separate, guiding principle of machine learning: whatever you do, you must maximally avoid training the model on the entire dataset rather than holding out a test split. In fact, you should be shamed if you report results which are obtained by training on the entire dataset rather than on the train split.

I want to argue that these are the same principle. Training against all of your alignment assessment techniques leads to the same failure as training on your validation data in traditional machine learning: you potentially get better performance, but you sacrifice all ability to verify your model’s behavior.

Consider two types of alignment techniques:

  1. Some techniques sculpt the model’s alignment. This includes techniques such as:
    1. Steering and other inference-time interventions
    2. SFT generalization techniques (midtraining, pretraining filters)
    3. RL generalization techniques (RLHF, RLAIF, beneficial RL, GRAFT, inoculation prompting)
    4. Prompt engineering
    5. Inference time safety classifiers
  2. Some techniques assess the model’s alignment (aka, monitoring). This includes techniques such as:
    1. Human analysis of model outputs
    2. CoT monitoring
    3. Activation monitoring
    4. Broader interp tools like SAEs, transcoders, etc.
    5. Evals for whether models can control their activations
    6. Pre-fill analysis
    7. Honeypots
    8. Universal jailbreaks (to study what the model will do at the limit)

All of these methods for sculpting a model's alignment can be repurposed for assessing its alignment, and vice versa. To give a few illustrative examples:

  1. Chain of thought:
    1. We can train models to not verbalize scheming by training against CoT monitors
    2. We can use CoT monitors to tell whether models are scheming
  2. Human feedback:
    1. We can RLHF models to behave according to human preferences
    2. We can hold out these human analyses to tell whether the model is behaving in ways people like.
  3. Probes
    1. We can train against deception probes to control the model’s actions
    2. We can deploy models with constitutional classifiers
  4. Honeypots
    1. We can train models to avoid honeypots
    2. We can hold out honeypots to see whether the model takes them
  5. Automated audits
    1. We can use automated auditing agents (petri) to find behaviors to RL away
    2. We can keep automated audits as a way to evaluate alignment
  6. The same can be said for gradient routing, RLAIF, data filtering, etc.

As soon as you train against the monitor (CoT, human feedback, probes, honeypots), you necessarily sacrifice this monitor's utility. The model now never admits misalignment which this monitor can catch, since many of the cases which were caught were trained away!

This holds trivially for CoT and honeypots, but it also applies to all the other alignment techniques. For instance, RLHF relies on human ‘monitors’ to catch bad responses so you can train them away. Filtering pretraining data relies on ‘monitors’ to identify samples that might cause bad generalization and then taking them out of the data mix.

At the limit—where you use all of the monitors for training and leave none for the test-set—you end up at extreme ‘you get what you measure’ problems: your model will necessarily appear aligned… because you’ve trained against everything which you might use to evaluate alignment!

The best (and only) example I know of where we’ve truly tried to hold out an alignment technique is chain of thought monitorability. However, CoT monitorability is dying and it would be exceedingly unwise to end up with no alignment techniques in our test set.

Importantly, the dataset of alignment techniques and the dataset of alignment environments is truly independent: we can train/test all of our alignment techniques using just a single alignment environment.

Consider a single standard reward-hacking honeypot. Within this one setting, one can train the model’s alignment by: training out verbalized scheming in the CoT, updating the model’s behavior based on human feedback, training the model’s behavior against a probe, RL-ing the model to avoid the honeypot, and training against automated audits seeded on this environment.

As a result, we essentially have two independent alignment datasets. We have some set of alignment samples: these are essentially the standard notion of data samples from machine learning. But we also have a set of alignment techniques: these are the way in which we update the model’s alignment using any one sample.

My point is this: models generalize across both alignment techniques and alignment samples. We hold out alignment samples all the time, but have significantly worse hygiene about train/test splits for alignment techniques.[1]

To operationalize the above ideas, consider this recent paper out of the Anthropic MATS stream.

In it, they propose a gradient routing mechanism—GRAFT—for removing misaligned behavior from a model. Their technique works by taking monitored (somewhat toy) RL envs and checking for reward hacks programmatically. If the hack occurred, you route the gradient update to a “Forget” adapter; otherwise, the update is routed to both the “Forget” adapter and a separate “Retain” adapter. With some optimization tricks, they show that you can then remove the Forget adapter during inference and (a) maintain good performance on the task while (b) observing less reward hacking.

Before going into my diatribe, I will emphasize that I like the idea of gradient routing and that I think it is good to explore this further as an alignment technique. I think it is better to have it than to not have it at all.

But my point is that it could work very well as an alignment testing technique. That is, instead of removing the adapter responsible for reward hacking, one can simply keep this adapter and, during inference, see whether the model routes computations through it. This would allow us to catch the model misbehaving.

However, this seems to have not been explored! If indeed GRAFT generalizes well to unseen reward hacks and this monitor absorbs all the ‘reward hackiness’ in the model, we should consider relegating it to exclusively being an alignment testing technique.

And, in either case, my more principled objection is that this does not solve the fundamental problem of alignment generalization. Regardless of whether you train against the monitor or you route gradients based on a monitor, you nonetheless have to rely on what the monitor can catch! And by removing the misalignments that this monitor observes, you render that monitor obsolete (e.g., you shrink your test set).

A natural objection is: “if we have methods for assuring alignment, why shouldn’t we train models using all of them? Won’t this make our models more aligned than if we didn’t?”

On the one hand, yes – training on your entire dataset will give you a better model than training on some subset of that data. But training on the entire dataset also renders you unable to determine if your resulting model is fundamentally flawed.

By not having a test-set, you are relegated to identifying alignment via trial-and-error during deployment. However, in the AGI regime, we cannot rely on alignment by trial and error. Indeed, AI alignment is the scientific discipline where we must respect the train/test split the most. ASI alignment has the property where our ‘ability to understand the model’ is directly commensurate with the extinction of the human race.

What does it mean to be better about this?

First, we must require transparency from frontier AI companies about which, if any, alignment techniques are relegated for testing. For instance, I’d love to be able to answer the following simple question: “what kinds of alignment RL do the frontier AI companies use”? Are they just training against every misalignment they can identify, in every way they possibly can? Or is there at least one clean, truly-held-out set of alignment environments and techniques which the model has never seen, where we can actually evaluate the model’s behavior? This won’t solve everything, but it would be way better than what we currently have.

Second, we should have a culture where we try to determine whether an alignment technique is better suited towards alignment training or alignment testing. For instance, RLHF seems quite good at alignment sculpting while CoT monitoring seems inherently alignment-assurance flavored. Some are less clear – for instance, it seems like people are training against activation monitors, but it also seems inherently risky to do so. In cases where it’s unclear, we should prioritize studying whether this is a train-set or a test-set idea.

Third, we should maximize our set of alignment techniques and prioritize that a large portion be sequestered for test purposes. This is why adopting looped transformer architectures is such a profoundly terrible decision – not only does it remove a valuable alignment technique, it got rid of one which was assurance-shaped!

Thanks to Sam Martin, Dewi Gould, Tim Hua, Jonathan Bostock, Mikael Høgsgaard and Moritz Pfau for comments & discussion. Thanks also to Raymond Douglas and Daniel Tan for lightly pressuring me to finally post this.


  1. ^

    Perhaps I'm belaboring the point here, but I really feel this strongly!



Discuss

item.title: Where ASI Could Stumble
item.description:
Before our eyes, forecasts are contracting and RSI is becoming nearer with each day. That's why I decided to publish a wide list of the obstacles for AI progress. I've been collecting these ideas for a long time, trying to make the list as comprehensive as it can be.

Some of these obstacles may turn out to be almost irrelevant. Others might slow things down by months or even longer. Or they might not. It's difficult to estimate their impact, so for now my goal was just to briefly list them.

List will include more then just obvious things like market correction, hardware shortages, or diminishing returns. Those are here too, of course. But also there are a few things that don't get a lot of attention.

I will start with the ones I consider as less interesting (part I) and move on to the more unusual variants (parts II & III).

I. Physical and Economic Bottlenecks

1. Energy limits

Developers announce campuses in gigawatts, file for interconnection and publish target dates that rarely survive permitting, financing and power supply.

- Energy Aspects

2. Hardware limits

IDC expects industry wafer capacity to grow by about 80% in 2027, while demand grows close to 2x.

- IDC

3. Market correction

Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction.

- IMF

4. Lack of training data

Actually, I don't personally consider this as a bottleneck. AI could learn from synthetic data or simulations without running into model collapse. We might also discover ways to train models more efficiently on the data we already have. Systems with continuous learning may emerge. After all, humans still generate thousands of petabytes of new data every day.

Additional:

There's also a tacit knowledge: knowledge that hasn't been formalized and is therefore difficult to transfer. But there's an obvious objection: AI can generalize beyond its training data. The real question is how well it can do that.

5. Political restrictions

Moratoriums on data center construction, regulations, export controls, and so on. The recent Democratic victory in the midterms makes me a bit more hopeful that this could become a meaningful obstacle.

6. Hardware performance ceiling

Even if an intelligence explosion happens, AI might still be limited by the performance of the hardware available at that moment. It would have to either come up with more energy-efficient algorithms or design new hardware and wait for it to be manufactured.

II. Algorithmic Constraints and Research Bottlenecks

7. Limits of distributed training

a) Data transfer within enormous clusters. Adding more compute eventually gives diminishing returns. Epoch has modeled potential data-movement bottlenecks.

b) Memory wall. Even if a processor is fast, memory bandwidth can still be a bottleneck. This problem is as old as time, or at least much older than AI.

8. Messy tasks

Training AI, especially with RL, is much harder when we're dealing with messy tasks where verifying the result is difficult, or where there's no single correct answer.
It's much easier to train an AI to solve math or programming problems than to teach it something like investing or running a large company.
I'd also put the famous problem of research taste here. It's not obvious how well something like that can be trained through RL.

9. Reliability on long-horizon tasks

Success rates depend on how long a task is, something METR has been tracking closely. Anyway, time horizons are steadily increasing. But the question is, will AI be able to handle tasks that take months or even years, especially if it has never encountered anything like them in its training data? This is related to the previous point.

There are also problems with long-term memory, context windows filling up, and so on.

10. Swarm scaling

A thousand researchers don't make research a thousand times faster. Five people won't make one cup of coffee five times faster than one person. For example, agents can duplicate each other's work.

Toby Ord estimated that increasing the number of agents by 10x produced gains equivalent to giving a single agent only 3-5x more reasoning tokens.

Additional:

a) Communication complexity. For some computational problems, there's a minimum amount of information that Alice and Bob have to exchange to solve the problem together, no matter how clever their protocol is.

b) Correlated failures. A lack of diversity: a million copies of the same model would stumble upon the same weaknesses.

11. Critical path

Sometimes you can't finish step C before getting the result of B, which itself depends on A, and so on. The related thing is Amdahl's law: the speedup you can get from parallelization is ultimately limited by the part of the work that can't be parallelized.

12. Sequential inference bottleneck

Transfomers generate text sequentially. Each new token depends on the tokens that came before it. Still, there is things like speculative decoding.

13. Experimental verification bottlenecks

Coming up with an idea is easier than verifying it. Experiments in the real world still take time, and in AI R&D there is a lot of experiments.

The same applies for new training runs, which can sometime take months.

14. Sample complexity

For some problems, there are mathematically proven lower bounds on the number of observations needed.

15. Diminishing returns themselves

And of course, there's the idea that finding each new useful idea requires more and more research effort.

On the other hand, a recent paper showed that automating research can create positive feedback loops strong enough to overcome diminishing returns.

III. Possible Fundamental Limits

16. Computational complexity

Some problems require massive amounts of computation in the worst case.

17. Computational irreducibility

For some processes, there may be no faster way to predict how they will evolve than to actually run through the process itself.

18. Chaos and limited predictability

Because of chaos, tiny uncertainties in initial conditions can grow very quickly. I'm not sure that even superintelligence could do a long-term predictions about certain physical systems.

19. Physical limits of computation

The Landauer limit, Bekenstein bound, Margolus–Levitin theorem, and the speed of light. These are all discussed in Seth Lloyd's classic paper.

Of course, if these are the only things left that limit superintelligence, our forecasts probably won't mean anything anymore. I'm including them as honourable mentions.



Discuss

item.title: Reading Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
item.description:
In 1964 [1], I. J. Good wrote Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine. I've only ever seen it cited for a single paragraph:

Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an "intelligence explosion," and the intelligence of man would be left far behind ... Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. It is curious that this point is made so seldom outside of science fiction. It is sometimes worthwhile to take science fiction seriously.

This is becoming increasingly relevant, with the AI Futures Project now estimating an intelligence explosion starting in 2027 in response to recent AI progress in automating AI research. Making our 'last invention' relinquishes our influence over the future, we have to get it right, and with the current frantic pace disastrous mistakes are likely.

I think the appropriate reaction to this news is something like "this is completely irresponsible, you're way too likely to get us all killed, do not do that" and marching in the streets (hence yesterday's protest attendance). But as someone who is very interested in how people process ideas and what they thought with the information they had at the time, my reaction also includes wanting to know more about what Good expected six decades ago.

I spent this morning reading his paper and talking about it with Claude (Fable 5.2). I was curious how the ideas had held up, what he got right, and what he got wrong. Some of his ideas were very technical, and not being an ML expert I can't add much there; I've put these in a Claude-authored appendix.

The first sentence reads very differently now:

The survival of man depends on the early construction of an ultraintelligent machine.

I think he was saying that he was worried that without one we'd kill ourselves off (later he writes "it will give the human race a good chance of surviving indefinitely"). This was during the Cold War, a couple years after the Cuban Missile Crisis, and before any agreement to limit (let alone reduce) nuclear stockpiles.

But now I'd interpret it the other way around: our survival depends on 'early construction' the same way that a driver's survival depends on how quickly they drive.

Reading further, the most-quoted paragraph still jumps out, and not just through familiarity. Reading it closely, the "provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control" is actually pretty prescient: he's essentially describing the plan of record, as much as there is one. Have AI research how to align AI. (This might work! But it also might not.)

He's also uncertain about whether it will go well. In the famous paragraph above he has a "provided that the machine is docile enough", later he says "the sign is uncertain" (math-speak for "could be good or bad"), and speculates whether "the human race will become redundant". He does seem overall optimistic, though, both in the 'survival depends' quote (above) and a few other places. For example, "the machines will create social problems, but they might also be able to solve them in addition to those that have been created by microbes and men."

A live objection at the time was that there wasn't any reason to make AI, and he cites B. V. Bowden's view that "it is easier to construct human brains by the usual method" before responding:

This shows that highly intelligent people can overlook the "intelligence explosion." It is true that it would be uneconomical to build a machine capable only of ordinary intellectual attainments, but it seems fairly probable that if this could be done then, at double the cost, the machine could exhibit ultraintelligence.

I'd actually count this as a bit of a miss: a machine capable of human-level work that was massively cheaper than humans could still be highly economical, and that's essentially what today's deployment of AI is. I suspect he didn't anticipate the extent to which high throughput would precede high intelligence.

I also don't see where his "double the cost" is coming from, and in practice this jump is likely to be much larger. But the critical thing he gets right is that human-level isn't a ceiling, and in a series of domains (games, coding, cybersecurity, math...) we've seen AI, after spending a while at "toy" and some time at "useful tool", quickly pass "human level" to get to something much more capable. I expect this keeps going.

On the technical side, most of the details are in Claude's appendix but at a high level it seems like he was right about a lot of how we got here. He thought it would be "vast artificial neural circuitry" and expected it would learn from experience and reinforcement:

Yet a detailed knowledge of semantics might not be required, since the artificial neural network will largely take care of it, provided that the parameters are correctly chosen, and provided that the network is adequately integrated with its sensorium and motorium (input and output). For, if these conditions are met, the machine will be able to learn from experience, by means of positive and negative reinforcement, and the instruction of the machine will resemble that of a child.

He also anticipated how text-based this would all be:

Whether a machine of classical or ultraparallel design is to be the first ultraintelligent machine, it will need to be able to handle or to learn to handle ordinary language with great facility. This will be important in order that its instructor should be able to teach it rapidly, and so that later the machine will be able to teach the instructor rapidly. It is very possible also that natural languages, or something analogous to them rather than to formal logic, are an essential ingredient of scientific imagination. Also the machine will be called upon to translate languages, and perhaps to generate fine prose and poetry at high speed, so that, all in all, linguistic facility is at a high premium.

He also correctly anticipated that AIs would use traditional computers (still then in their infancy) as tools, with coding and search:

In any event the ultraintelligent machine might as well have a large electronic computer at its beck and call, and also a multimillion dollar information-retrieval installation of large capacity but of comparatively slow speed, since these would add little to the total cost.

And he anticipated a period before AI fully surpassed humans, during which they'd work together:

Until an ultraintelligent machine is built perhaps the best intellectual feats will be performed by men and machines in very close, sometimes called "symbiotic," relationship

This is how many of us work daily, including both my day job and these blog posts.

He was also a strong chess player (on the Bletchley Chess Club during the war) and suggested:

so-called "randomized chess," in which the positions of the white pieces on the first rank are permuted at random before the game begins (but with the two bishops on squares of opposite colors), and then the initial positions of the black pieces are determined by mirror symmetry. This gives rise to 1440 essentially distinct initial positions and effectively removes from the game the effect of mere parrot learning of the openings

This is very close to Chess960 (though without the extra castling work) which Bobby Fischer proposed decades later, and I was initially pretty excited to see it. But reading more it turns out this was a known variant going back centuries. Good's including it here to illustrate that what we really care about is the reasoning component of chess, not memorizing opening lines.

Thinking about things Good got wrong, the timing initially seems like a big one: "more probable than not ... within the twentieth century". But he only put it at 50%, and while it has taken longer it looks like it's going much faster than most others predicted.

A much larger miss is the cost of artificial neurons:

If we could raise say a hundred billion dollars we might be able to simulate all the neurons of a brain, and of a whole man, at a cost of ten dollars per artificial neuron.

Since Moore's law is newer than Good's writing it's not surprising that he didn't fully account for it (though he did expect "great advances in microminiaturization"), but the hardware to power an artificial neuron costs ~10,000x less than this (~$0.01 in current dollars, less if you quantize; Good's $10 would be ~$100 today).

On the other hand, and more importantly, he's in the right ballpark on total cost: the world has spent maybe $1T to date creating AI systems and I expect we spend maybe that again by the end of 2027 as recursive self-improvement increases the returns to AI R&D. Good's $100B is $1T in current dollars, but note that he didn't expect anyone to pay this:

But it seems unlikely that more than say [$300M then; $3B today] would actually be forthcoming, and even this amount might be difficult to obtain without first building the machine!

This is indeed how funding has worked, with investors putting in more money in response to initial progress. That he ended up close to right on the ~$1T looks to me like less of a coincidence than it appears: costs come down over time, and it's only when they're getting into an economically feasible range that someone might actually do it.

The biggest miss, though, is about focus. He was super early in thinking about whether such a machine would be good for the world, but then spends almost the entire paper on how one might be designed. Focusing on the "how" and not the "whether" is very normal for technical people then and now, and as an engineer I feel this pull as well. But it's something people have been getting wrong since the beginning: excitement about the potential, not staring hard at the true scale of the risk.

This paper isn't the last we have of Good's thinking, however, and in 1998 he provided a bio to the IEEE on receiving their Computer Pioneer Award. It doesn't seem to have been used at the ceremony or published, but James Barrat says Good's assistant Leslie Pendleton gave him a copy, and Barrat quotes it in his 2013 Our Final Invention. Note that this is Good writing about himself in the third person:

"The survival of man depends on the early construction of an ultra-intelligent machine." Those were his words during the Cold War, and he now suspects that "survival" should be replaced by "extinction." He thinks that, because of international competition, we cannot prevent the machines from taking over.

How to get countries to coordinate to prevent the machines from taking over is a key question today.

Appendix: Good's technical predictions I asked Claude Fable 5.2 to write an appendix. The judgments are its own, and I haven't checked them:

Most of Good's paper is a theory of how a neural network could store meaning and recall it. Below I go through its main technical claims and say how well I think each matches how current AI systems work. I grade each as a strong match, a partial match, a loose match, or a miss.

Two cautions first. A 58-page speculative paper makes a lot of claims, and picking out the ones that look right in hindsight flatters it. And Good was less of a lone voice than this list might suggest. Neural networks were an active research area in the early 1960s: he cites Rosenblatt's perceptron work, and builds on Hebb, Ashby, and Shannon. His bet was on one of the two live approaches, the one that then went out of fashion for decades and eventually won.

Learning is adjusting connection strengths. Strong match. In his radio-linked machine (p35, p36):

The strength of the connection could be represented by the accuracy of the tuning. ... "Positive reinforcement" would correspond to improved tuning of these filters.
Every connection has an adjustable strength, and learning means changing the strengths. That is what a "weight" is in a modern network, and training is nothing more than adjusting weights.

How the strengths get adjusted. Miss. Good's rule (p80) is that a connection has a small random chance of stepping up in strength whenever it is "successfully used (i.e., contributes to the activation or inhibition of an artificial neuron)". This is a local rule: each connection changes based only on its own activity. Modern networks are trained by backpropagation, which works out how every weight in the network contributed to an error in the final output and adjusts them all together. Nothing in the paper anticipates this, and local rules of Good's kind have not been made to work at scale.

What "reinforcement" means. Partial match. Jeff asked whether Good's "positive and negative reinforcement" from an instructor is what is now called reinforcement learning from human feedback. It does resemble it, and that technique is used to shape how current models behave. But most of what those models know comes from a different source, predicting the next word across a vast amount of text. Good's usage is broader than reward from an instructor. The rule above involves no instructor, he says the machine is educated only "partly" by reinforcement (p80), and his account of the child is about exposure:

The child later associates words with objects and activities, by implicit statistical inference ... At a later stage of linguistic development, similar statistical associations are developed between linguistic elements themselves. (p45, p46)
He has the right raw material, the statistics of which words occur with what, and he discusses predicting words from the preceding ones (p43, p54). He never proposes prediction as the thing to train on.

Words are known by the company they keep. Strong match, though not original to him.

The essential idea is that words can be seen to be associated not merely because they occur frequently together, but because they both occur frequently in conjunction with a third word (p71)
His example is that "ferry" and "fare" are related because both go with words like "bus". This is the basis of how modern systems represent word meaning. Linguists (Harris, Firth) had stated the idea in the 1950s. What Good adds is the argument that a machine needs it, since machines that "rely only on frequencies" (p71) can say nothing about combinations they haven't seen.

Word vectors. Partial match. On p52 and p53 he takes a table of how often each word occurs in each document, takes logarithms, subtracts a constant from each row and column, and proposes decomposing the result so that

This would associate a w-dimensional vector with each index term and with each document. The relevance of index term i to document j could now be defined as the correlation coefficient between the two associated vectors.
This is recognizably the method later known as latent semantic analysis (around 1990), and a relative of the word-embedding methods of the 2010s, which were shown to be doing something close to factoring a similar table. Two things are missing. He keeps as many dimensions as there are words, where the later methods get their power from keeping only a few hundred. And the vectors are computed once, not learned by a network. He also offers it only as "another conceivable method" and judges the computation "exceedingly great".

Generalization is the central problem. Strong match on the diagnosis, partial on the cure.

One of the main difficulties in this subject is how to estimate the probabilities of events that have never occurred. That such probabilities are relevant to intelligence is to be expected, since intelligence is sometimes defined as the ability to adapt to new circumstances. (p32)
This is still the right way to state it. Good had worked on this problem with Turing, and the resulting method (Good-Turing estimation) was a standard component of statistical language models into the 2000s. Current models don't use it. They generalize by learning that similar words and situations behave similarly, which is closer to his "ferry" and "fare" idea, and to his remark (p71) that getting the network to form abstractions is "one of the most vital problems".

What comes next depends on recent context and stored weights. Partial match. Good's unit of thought is the "assembly", Hebb's term for a group of neurons that fire together and stand for a word or idea.

Which assembly becomes active at the next moment must depend on the current sensory input, the current dominant assembly, and the currently active subassemblies. Indirectly, therefore, it depends on the recent assembly sequence, wherein the most recent assemblies will have the greatest influence. It also depends of course on the semipermanent static storage, the "past history." (p60)
A language model has the same division: what comes next is determined by the recent text it is looking at (its "context") and by weights fixed during training. Good's list of memory types (p72) puts short-term memory in current activity and long-term memory in connection strengths, which is the same split, and he says a long "attention span" is "certainly essential for intelligence" (p63). He goes on (p66) to score each candidate next assembly as a baseline plus a contribution from each recent one, with the highest total firing. The last step of a language model has that form, a score for every possible next word. But in a modern model the contributions from earlier words interact in complicated ways before that step, and Good only gestures at this by saying interaction terms will be needed (p67). I wouldn't claim more than a family resemblance.

Concepts are spread across many neurons. Strong match, shared credit.

each neuron would occur in a great many distinct circuits, and would not be indispensable for any of them. (p56)
He contrasts this with "one concept, one neuron". Modern networks store concepts as patterns over many units, with each unit taking part in many concepts, and this is a main reason their workings are hard to read off. The idea came from neuroscience (he cites Lashley and Eccles). Good's contribution is an efficiency argument for it, by analogy with a punched-card coding scheme.

Keep probabilities, not hard decisions. Strong match. Section 3 argues that a system understanding speech should pass along graded probabilities between its levels instead of committing to one answer at each, because "each definite 'decision' loses information" (p39). Modern networks pass continuous values between layers and only commit at the output.

Rejecting a logical "canonical language". Strong match. He considers representing meaning by translating every statement into a standard formal form, and concludes this would be "extremely difficult, perhaps even logically impossible, or perhaps it would require an ultraintelligent machine to do it!" (p41). Large projects later attempted roughly this and did not get far. Relatedly, his guess (p36, quoted in the main post) that natural language "rather than ... formal logic" is needed for scientific imagination is a partial match: current models do much of their reasoning by writing out steps in ordinary language.

Scale can substitute for design. Partial match.

a well-designed machine of say 109 components might be educable to ultraintelligence, but a much more carelessly designed machine of say 1013 components might be equally good. (p62)
The history of the field broadly supports this: simple methods given more computation have repeatedly beaten cleverer ones. But Good, following Ashby, bases it on the hope that almost any large, richly connected network will behave intelligently. That turned out to be false. Scale paid off only once there was a training method able to make use of it.

The hard part is ape-level intelligence. Partial match. He says "most of the struggle" will be building "a machine with the intelligence of an ape" (p45), because perception and basic learning are harder than what comes after. In favor: getting networks to learn to see took until about 2012, and fluent language followed within a decade. Against: language arrived without anything like an ape's physical competence, and robotics is still behind.

Sleep and replay. Partial match. His conjecture that sleep serves "to replay the assembly sequences that were of greatest interest during the day in order to consolidate them" (p80) is close to a well-supported view in neuroscience. In AI, replaying stored experience, with priority to the most informative parts, is a standard technique in systems that learn by trial and error. It is not part of how language models are mainly trained, so his suggestion that the machine would "benefit from periods of comparative rest" (p72) is a loose match at best.

Understanding as economy. Loose match. He argues that storing meanings instead of exact wordings saves a great deal of memory, and that this may be "the evolutionary function of meaning and understanding" (p77). There is a real modern parallel, since learning to predict text well and learning to compress it are mathematically the same task. Good's argument is about storage, though, and I think the connection is more suggestive than exact.

Hardware. Mixed. He was right that serial speed alone wouldn't do. He expected computers to become about a million times faster than neurons and still concluded the machine "will need to be ultraparallel" (p35), and current systems do depend on massively parallel chips. He was right that low power consumption "will be valuable" (p33). He was wrong that the neurons would be physical devices. They are simulated in software.

The brain as blueprint. Mostly a miss. The paper opens by saying that to design the machine "we need to understand more about the human brain or human thought or both", and later that brain anatomy is "very relevant" (p63). Current systems borrow the neuron and the adjustable connection and almost nothing else. Of the brain theory itself, Hebb's assemblies remain a respected idea in neuroscience, but the central control system Good relies on (taken from Penfield) has been abandoned, and his own extensions haven't been taken up. To his credit, he says the designer will have to guess which features of the brain matter, and he allows that the first machine might not use a neural network after all (p78).

Theory before experiment. Miss.

The need for further theory is great, since, without advances in theory, the amount of experimentation might be prohibitive. (p64)
Computation became cheap enough to experiment at enormous scale, and the systems we have were found that way. Theory explaining why they work is still well behind.

How much the machine needs to learn from. Miss. He sizes the machine's education to a person's: "A man cannot learn more than ten million statements in a lifetime" (p36). Current models learn much less from each example than people do, and compensate with volume. By my rough estimate they are trained on something like ten thousand times more text than a person could read in a lifetime.

Overall. Good was right about the kind of thing the machine would be: a very large, parallel neural network that learns the meanings of words from statistics, stores them as distributed patterns, treats generalization as the core problem, and works in natural language with conventional computers as tools. He was wrong, or silent, about how such a network could actually be trained, which is the part that took the field another fifty years. I'd put his reputation for foresight on these pages at least as much as on the famous paragraph.

[1] I generally see 1965, including on Wikipedia probably because of the publication date. But I think it's more informative to count by the date he wrote it: "The first draft of this monograph was completed in April 1963, and the present slightly amended version in May 1964."
